meeting_header: Date: 2027-02-16 | Time: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 45 min | Attendees: Avery (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Samir (Redwood SE), Diego (SummitCore CTO), Priya (ML Eng), Liam (Infra), Hannah (SRE)
summary: Weekly POC sync to review latest benchmark runs comparing Redwood inference against SummitCore's incumbent provider. Discussed latency p50/p95 deltas, throughput at target concurrency, KV cache hit behavior, quantization artifacts, and next steps: spin up stress slot, share full bench spreadsheet, security docs, and finalize pricing scenarios.
topics: KV cache hit rates and prefix caching
transcript:
[00:00] Avery (Redwood): alright good afternoon everyone, thanks for joining, um we're gonna run through the latest lab results from this week and then make a clear list of next steps. Maya is gonna share the bench summary.
[00:12] Maya (Redwood SE): hey all, hi Diego, Priya, Liam — quick context, we re-ran three classes of prompts: short chit-chat, medium-context resolution (300-600 tokens), and long doc-summarize (1.2k tokens). runs were with the quantized-medium profile (int8-ish) on A100 equivalent infra for Redwood. baseline runs were from the incumbent — we label them CloudVendorX in the sheets.
[00:35] Diego (SummitCore): ok sounds good. just to confirm the target we care about is p95 under 500ms for short and medium right?
[00:42] Priya (SummitCore): yes p95 <500 for short/medium; for long we're okay up to about 1.2s as long as cost is reasonable.
[00:50] Maya: right. quick numbers: short prompts p50 Redwood 120ms vs baseline 170ms; p95 Redwood 310ms vs baseline 470ms. medium prompts p50 230ms vs 300ms; p95 420ms vs 610ms. long prompts p50 750ms vs 920ms; p95 1.1s vs 1.7s. overall unit token cost we measured ~18% lower on Redwood for the quantized profile in this lab depending on batching.
[01:25] Liam (Infra): ok those deltas look promising, can you explain batch sizes and concurrency during the runs?
[01:30] Maya: sure, we ran three concurrency sweeps: low (8 concurrent reqs), mid (32), high (96). batching policy for Redwood runtime is adaptive, but we forced batch caps of 32 and 128 to simulate heavy tail. KV cache was enabled for medium/long runs, observed hit-rate ~64% for medium when we used prefix caching between similar prompts; baseline showed ~50% hit-rate — likely due to Redwood's prefix grouping and continuous batching.
[01:58] Samir (Redwood): and that higher cache hit translates to less decode work, so p95 improvement is magnified for typical conversational flow. worth noting the baseline has slightly higher single-thread decode performance but suffers at scale because of less effective batching and cache reuse.
[02:15] Priya: the p95 numbers are great, but can you show variability? like percent of runs that were >600ms for medium prompts?
[02:22] Maya: yes, in the sheet we have a histogram — for medium prompts, Redwood had ~7% of runs >600ms at high concurrency, baseline had ~18%. the tail is where you see the biggest difference.
[02:34] Diego: did you change the model? are you serving an identical family? I want to be sure we're comparing apples to apples.
[02:40] Maya: we're using the same model checkpoint family; the differences are quantization profile and kernel selection. Redwood used an fp16->int8 hybrid quant path for attention kernels which saves memory and improves throughput. baseline used a generic int8 path but without the same kernel tiling optimizations. small tokenization differences may exist from different tokenizers but we normalised token counts in the spreadsheet.
[03:05] Hannah (SRE): any observed hallucination or quality regressions with quantization? Priya, have you looked at the eval prompts?
[03:12] Priya: we spot-checked 200 outputs — no obvious regressions in the key intents. there are minor truncation artifacts on very long completions with aggressive quant, but for our production prompts it's acceptable. we'll run a broader QA pass.
[03:26] Liam: what's the GPU util during those high concurrency tests? we need to understand margin for burst.
[03:31] Maya: GPU util averaged 78% in mid and 92% at high concurrency; baseline was pegged above 95% more often which explains the higher tail. Redwood's kernel scheduling and smaller memory footprint left more headroom for batching.
[03:50] Samir: also worth noting the throughput numbers — tokens/sec per GPU: Redwood median 12.6k tps at mid, 9.8k at high (because of increased per-request overhead), baseline 10.4k mid, 7.1k high. so at scale Redwood sustained better throughput with lower p95.
[04:10] Diego: are these numbers captured under the same sequence length distribution? appraisal?
[04:15] Maya: yes we used the same synthetic sequence distribution derived from SummitCore's production traces (you provided those), buckets: 20% short, 60% medium, 20% long.
[04:24] Priya: what about cold-starts and KV priming? some of our flows do infrequent long-context calls that'll prime the KV a lot.
[04:31] Maya: cold-start p95 is worse by design — initial decode cost is higher. we recommend a lightweight warm cache strategy for those flows or a small kept-warm pool / low-cost reserved slot to keep key contexts alive. that reduces cold p95 by ~30% in our tests.
[04:48] Liam: curious about networking — what's the egress latency contribution? if we do VPC peering, can we cut another 20-40ms?
[04:55] Samir: yes, in our lab most runs were in-region with ~15ms avg network overhead. With VPC peering and direct connect it's commonly sub-5ms in our internal tests, so you'll see an extra tail improvement. we'll include a network delta estimate in the bench sheet.
[05:12] Diego: how confident are we in cost deltas? the 18% lower unit cost sounds great but our procurement will want a modeled monthly spend at 500 million tokens.
[05:20] Avery: good question — we'll produce a modeled delta sheet: hosted vs dedicated amortizing reserved capacity. early estimate: if you commit to a moderate dedicated pool (3-4 GPUs for baseline QPS) you could see 30-35% lower op-ex overall vs incumbent, once you factor reserved pricing and higher cache efficiency. I'll put concrete numbers in the spreadsheet.
[05:41] Priya: one thing — for long-form summarization, do you recommend switching quant profile or disabling quant? we saw more truncation artifacts in long logs.
[05:49] Maya: for long-form we recommend a mixed approach: keep attention/tile kernels higher precision (fp16) and quantize the feed-forward path. that keeps coherence while still saving memory. performance drops slightly but p95 remains within your 1.2s target in our tests.
[06:05] Diego: any red flags for compliance or data retention in Redwood Private mode? though we're initially evaluating hosted.
[06:11] Avery: for Private we offer a customer-managed control plane, KMS integration, audit logs. we'll send the SOC2/ISO pack and a note on how KMS/HSM key rotation would look. Liam, Hannah — you'll want to review the VPC peering and HSM access pattern doc.
[06:27] Hannah: yes please. also SLA questions — if we push to production with critical SLA, can you support automatic fallback to baseline during incidents?
[06:33] Samir: yes — Redwood runtime supports policy-based fallback to compatible model variants or to a different routing target. we've used that in other pilots, we can demo it if you want.
[06:44] Priya: ok next steps on our side — we'll run a QA sweep on the output set and share the canonical sample prompts tomorrow. Diego will pull procurement requirements.
[06:53] Diego: yep. we'll also confirm a nominal QPS target for the final performance gate.
[06:59] Avery: great. Maya, can you confirm the stress slot plan and the GPU spec?
[07:03] Maya: yes, plan is to spin up a 4x A100-equivalent dedicated slot with quantized-medium and fp16-long profiles, run a 2-hour stress test with ramping concurrency, and capture traces and kernel-level profiling. we'll deliver the result sheet and raw traces. target to execute on 2027-02-18 morning.
[07:20] Liam: small ask — can you include syslogs and a sample flamegraph for the worst-case p95 run so our infra can triage?
[07:26] Samir: yes we'll include flamegraphs and a CPU/GPU timeline for the top 5 worst runs.
[07:31] Priya: and please annotate where tokenization differences might have affected latency.
[07:35] Maya: will do.
[07:37] Avery: ok let's recap: Redwood to share updated bench spreadsheet with per-prompt class p50/p95 histograms, send SOC2/KMS notes, provision stress slot 2027-02-18, pricing scenarios by 2027-02-17, and follow up call 2027-02-23. Anything else?
[07:53] Diego: nope that's it, thanks everyone. seems like we have a clear path to a performance gate.
[07:58] Hannah: thanks, bye.
[08:00] Maya: thanks all, bye.

Note: transcription contains occasional mis-attributions and minor word errors, see bench sheet for raw numbers and graphs.
